summary: This document describes how to use Suite B cryptography with Secure Shell, using elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman, ECDSA, and AES in Galois/Counter Mode. Suite B was a US government set of algorithms. The RFC has historic status.

plainLanguage.summary: Suite B was a government-approved set of secret-code tools. This explained how to use them with SSH, but it is now historic and kept for the record.

questions: ssh with ecdh and ecdsa suite b
how does suite b use elliptic curves
subtitle: Using US government cryptography standards with the Secure Shell protocol.

tldr.problem: The US government published Suite B, a set of cryptographic algorithms for national security applications, but SSH implementations needed guidance on how to use only those algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how to build an SSH implementation using elliptic curve cryptography (ECDH and ECDSA), AES in Galois/Counter Mode for encryption and authentication, and SHA-2 hashes, restricted to government-approved curves and key sizes.
tldr.outcome: Suite B is now Historic as government cryptography policies evolved. The RFC serves as a reference for how government systems applied Suite B to SSH during the period when the policy was active.

today: RFC 6239 is Historic. It describes how to use Suite B, a government cryptographic policy that was active when the RFC was published. The policy has since evolved, and Suite B specifications are maintained for reference by systems that need to support legacy configurations.

sections.title: Suite B and the SSH Protocol
sections.content:
Suite B was a set of cryptographic algorithms approved by the United States government for protecting national security information. This RFC describes how to use Suite B components with the Secure Shell (SSH) protocol, which is used to remotely log into computers and transfer files securely.

Suite B SSH uses four main cryptographic primitives: Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) for key agreement between client and server, Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) for authentication, AES in Galois/Counter Mode (AES-GCM) for both encrypting data and checking that it has not been tampered with, and the SHA-2 family of hash functions (SHA-256 and SHA-384). All of these are based on elliptic curve mathematics instead of older algorithms like RSA or traditional Diffie-Hellman.

The document specifies two levels of security strength: a 128-bit minimum level using the P-256 elliptic curve, and a 192-bit minimum level using the P-384 curve.
sections.plainLanguage: Suite B was the government's approved list of secret-code tools. This explains how to use them in SSH, the program you use to log into a faraway computer safely.

sections.title: Protocol Architecture and Message Flow
sections.content:
Suite B SSH follows the standard SSH message flow with key exchange, server authentication, user authentication, and data protection phases. During key exchange, the client and server use SSH_MSG_KEXINIT messages to negotiate which algorithms they both support; Suite B constrains these choices to the approved algorithms only. The client and server then perform Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key agreement using either the P-256 or P-384 curve, exchanged in SSH_MSG_KEXECDH_INIT and SSH_MSG_KEXECDH_REPLY messages.

The server proves its identity using an X.509 certificate containing its ECDSA public key and an ECDSA signature over the key exchange hash. For user authentication, the user must also use ECDSA with an X.509 certificate; at the 192-bit security level, P-384 signatures are required. Once the session keys are derived, all SSH binary packets are encrypted and authenticated using AES-GCM, which both protects confidentiality and detects any tampering. Either side can request a rekey, during which new keys are negotiated without changing the cipher suite.
sections.plainLanguage: During login, the computer and your computer trade secret numbers using fancy math (elliptic curves). Your computer checks the server's ID card (certificate). You prove who you are with your own ID card. Then all the traffic gets scrambled and tagged to spot if anyone's been snooping.

sections.title: Cryptographic Algorithm Choices
sections.content:
Suite B specifies two families of algorithms. Family 1 provides 128-bit strength using the P-256 curve with 128-bit AES and SHA-256. Family 2 provides up to 192-bit strength using the P-384 curve with 256-bit AES and SHA-384. At the 128-bit security level, implementations may use exclusively Family 1, exclusively Family 2, or support both; the choice is made during algorithm negotiation. At the 192-bit security level, only Family 2 is permitted.

For digital signatures and X.509 certificates, ECDSA-256 may be used to authenticate at the 128-bit level, but all implementations at the 192-bit level must support ECDSA-384. At the 192-bit level, ECDSA-384 may also authenticate ECDSA-256 keys, ensuring interoperability. The RFC specifies which algorithm combinations are allowed in the SSH_MSG_KEXINIT negotiation to prevent downgrade attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two strength levels: medium (128-bit) uses P-256 and 128-bit AES, while high (192-bit) uses P-384 and 256-bit AES. The server and client have to agree on which level to use.

sections.title: Security Requirements and Implementation Concerns
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that when using elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman, each exponent (random secret) must have full entropy: 256 bits of entropy for P-256 and 384 bits for P-384. The AES-GCM mode implementation is critical: the invocation counter and block counter must be properly maintained to prevent key reuse, which would completely break the security.

The RFC also notes that Suite B SSH implementations must validate X.509 certificates back to a trusted root, and that either party may initiate a rekey at any time. All intermediate versions of SSH and SSH-related RFCs that have been used to build Suite B components are normatively referenced, ensuring that implementers check those documents for details that this RFC does not repeat.
sections.plainLanguage: The random numbers have to be really random, the counter that counts encryptions has to be exactly right, and the certificates have to prove they came from someone you trust.
